strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing memory benchmarks are largely static reading-comprehension tasks, while this work explicitly targets procedural memory built from simulated user feedback, which is a meaningful and underexplored angle.
Broad coverage: 11 public datasets spanning three domains (open, legal, academic), two languages, and four input/output length format combinations, unified into a common (q, v, c) schema.

Thorough feedback simulation design: explicit/implicit and verbose/action feedback types are grounded in prior IR/user-behavior literature, with a principled probabilistic mapping from satisfaction scores to like/dislike/copy actions calibrated against real usage statistics (Shuster et al., Chatterji et al.).

Extensive experimentation: off-policy, on-policy, and stepwise off-policy settings; multiple backbones (Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B); time/efficiency analysis; action-feedback-only and SFT ablations; all with substantial appendix detail supporting reproducibility.

Interesting and somewhat counter-intuitive empirical finding that SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) often underperform naive RAG baselines outside of the narrow long-context QA setting they were originally validated on, which is a useful corrective for the community.

Detailed efficiency analysis (Figure 3, Table 14) revealing pathological slowdowns in Mem0 and high latency in MemoryOS, which is valuable practical information often missing from prior memory-system papers.
Reproducibility efforts appear substantial: open-sourced scripts, simulators, evaluation pipelines, and released feedback logs, plus very detailed appendix documentation of prompts and datasets.
weaknesses: The core evaluation metric relies heavily on LLM-as-judge merging of multiple heterogeneous metrics into a single 1-10 score (for JuDGE, IdeaBench, SciTechNews, and most LiLo/SiLo LLM-as-judge datasets), yet no human validation, inter-rater agreement, or correlation analysis with human judgments is reported for this merging step or for the judge itself, which undermines confidence in the reliability of a large fraction of the reported numbers.

The user feedback simulator's reliability is validated primarily via the 'with vs without feedback' comparison and mostly on the trivial finding that feedback marginally improves same-turn regeneration; this does not establish that simulated feedback signals faithfully mirror real human feedback distributions or biases (e.g., real users' explicit feedback is much rarer/noisier and might correlate with different aspects than an LLM judge's notion of quality).

The overall aggregation methodology (min-max normalization/z-score averaged across heterogeneous datasets and metrics) is somewhat ad hoc, and the paper does not report variance/statistical significance across seeds or dataset splits, making it hard to assess whether observed differences between baselines (e.g., RAG vs. A-Mem) are robust or within noise, especially given the fluctuating on-policy/stepwise curves shown in the appendix (Figs 4-9) which show substantial non-monotonic swings.

Only one backbone family (Qwen3) is used for the main results, with Qwen3-32B tested only on a subset of domains; the generality of conclusions (e.g., 'memory-based LLMsys underperform naive RAG') across other backbone families (e.g., GPT-4o-class, Llama, Gemini) is untested, weakening claims of generalizability.

The taxonomy contribution (declarative/procedural, semantic/episodic, explicit/implicit feedback) is a synthesis of well-established concepts from psychology and IR rather than a novel technical framework, and the 'first benchmark with all types of memory and feedback' claim in Table 1 is more of a coverage checklist than evidence of qualitative superiority.

Explanations for why memory-based systems underperform naive RAG (e.g., 'existing memory-based LLMsys do not differentiate historical task logs from current task context') are plausible but not rigorously tested via targeted ablations isolating this specific hypothesis; the discussion remains largely speculative.

The paper's presentation is dense and the main text under-explains several important experimental design choices (e.g., precise definition of an 'on-policy step,' how batch size of 100 training cases interacts with the underlying dataset sizes, why on-policy curves are so noisy) that are only clarified deep in the appendix, hurting readability of the core submission.

Reproducibility statement mentions open-sourced code/data but the actual URLs are blank/omitted in the provided manuscript text, so verifying resource availability is not currently possible from the paper itself.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and important gap in existing LLM memory benchmarks, which mostly test static long-context reading comprehension rather than continual learning from accumulated user feedback during service.

Proposes a clear and useful taxonomy distinguishing declarative (semantic/episodic) vs. procedural memory and explicit (verbose/action) vs. implicit feedback, which helps organize a fragmented literature.
Builds a large, diverse benchmark spanning 11 datasets, 3 domains, 2 languages, and 4 input/output length combinations, substantially broader than prior memory benchmarks (Table 1).

Extensive and multi-faceted experimentation: off-policy, on-policy, stepwise off-policy, action-feedback-only, and different backbone sizes (Qwen3-8B/32B), plus detailed time-consumption/latency analysis of memory operations.

Reports interesting, somewhat counter-intuitive findings (e.g., SOTA memory systems like A-Mem/Mem0/MemoryOS often underperform naive RAG baselines across most partitions), which is a valuable, honest contribution to the field rather than simply promoting the authors' own method.
Detailed appendix with prompt templates, dataset processing details, and per-dataset metrics supports transparency of the evaluation pipeline.
weaknesses: The core claim that the LLM-as-user feedback is 'realistic' is not validated against real human feedback or human judgments; all validation of feedback quality (Table 11/12) is circular, using the same or similar LLMs both to generate and to judge outputs, which limits confidence in the benchmark's ecological validity.

The action-feedback probability model (like/dislike/copy rates) is calibrated using statistics from unrelated general chatbot usage studies (Chatterji et al., Shuster et al.) rather than derived from or validated for the specific tasks/domains in MemoryBench, so its realism for e.g. legal or academic writing tasks is unclear.

Merging heterogeneous metrics into a single LLM-as-judge score (for JuDGE, IdeaBench, SciTechNews, etc.) is a significant design choice whose reliability/validity (e.g., agreement with human raters) is not empirically verified.

Many reported trends (on-policy and stepwise off-policy curves in Figs. 4-9) are noisy and non-monotonic with no error bars or repeated runs, making it hard to distinguish genuine learning dynamics from measurement noise or randomness in sampling/generation.
The reproducibility statement contains blank/missing links for the data and code repositories, undermining the claimed openness at least in the reviewed version.

Only one primary backbone (Qwen3-8B, with limited Qwen3-32B checks) is used for all baselines; generalization of findings (e.g., that RAG rivals SOTA memory systems) to other model families/sizes is untested.

The performance gains attributed to feedback in Table 11 are often small in absolute terms (e.g., 0.0002–0.03 for many ROUGE/BERTScore-based metrics), raising questions about whether the observed 'usefulness of feedback' is practically meaningful versus statistical noise.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing LLM memory benchmarks (Locomo, DialSim, LongMemEval, etc.) mostly test static long-context reading comprehension, whereas MemoryBench specifically targets continual learning from accumulated user feedback (procedural memory), which is conceptually well-motivated by neuroscience/IR analogies.

Comprehensive taxonomy of memory (declarative/procedural, semantic/episodic) and feedback (explicit/implicit, verbose/action) types that is clearly articulated and used to systematically differentiate MemoryBench from prior work (Table 1, Table 3).

Broad empirical coverage: 11 public datasets spanning 3 domains, 2 languages, and 4 task-length formats, with a large and varied set of baselines (RAG variants, A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS, SFT) tested under both off-policy and on-policy settings.

The reported finding that SOTA memory systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) are frequently outperformed by naive RAG baselines is a useful, somewhat surprising negative result that could meaningfully inform future memory-system design, and is corroborated by additional analyses (per-dataset breakdowns, time-consumption profiling, action-feedback and noise-robustness experiments).

Substantial engineering effort toward reproducibility: released code, prompts, simulated feedback logs for off-policy learning, detailed appendix documentation of prompts, hyperparameters, and dataset-specific evaluation protocols.

Thoughtful attempt to validate the LLM-as-user feedback simulator via human annotation and via ablations comparing with/without feedback and varying noise levels, showing feedback generally helps performance.
weaknesses: The human evaluation used to justify that simulated feedback is 'indistinguishable' from human feedback has weak inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' Kappa 0.093 for naturalness, 0.27–0.38 for relevance/overall quality), which undercuts confidence in this claim; the paper's framing as strong supportive evidence is somewhat overstated given such low agreement.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge to merge heterogeneous metrics into a single 1-10 score and then min-max/normalize across systems and datasets is methodologically convenient but introduces additional noise/bias layers (judge model biases, arbitrary scaling) that are not deeply validated against human judgments beyond the feedback-quality study.

The satisfaction-score distribution used to calibrate the action-feedback simulator (Table 4) is heavily skewed toward high scores (musch of the mass in 7-9), and the sigmoid hyperparameters are calibrated from a couple of external, not-fully-comparable studies (Shuster et al., Chatterji et al.), raising questions about how representative the simulated action feedback is of real user populations across the very different domains tested.

Because all tested baselines (RAG, A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) are existing systems not designed for this benchmark's procedural-memory setting, the central finding that they underperform is somewhat expected/self-fulfilling; the paper offers no new algorithm or even a simple tailored baseline that better handles procedural memory, limiting the constructive/prescriptive value of the contribution beyond diagnosis.

Several dataset partitions and ablations (e.g., action-feedback experiments, some Academic/Legal subsets) use quite small sample sizes (as few as 82–250 cases), and on-policy experiments were only run for a subset of systems due to computational cost, which limits the statistical robustness of some comparative claims, particularly the volatile/inconsistent trends shown in the on-policy and stepwise off-policy curves that are not explained mechanistically.

Aggregation methodology (min-max normalization then averaging across heterogeneous datasets/metrics) can be sensitive to outliers and disproportionately weight datasets with different scales or score ranges, and the paper does not report sensitivity analysis or alternative aggregation strategies to check robustness of the main comparative conclusions.

Presentation could be improved: some repeated content/artifacts in the very long appendix, minor inconsistencies, and the main text's core comparative results (Figure 3) are dense and hard to parse without cross-referencing the appendix tables.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap in the literature: existing memory benchmarks focus on static declarative/episodic knowledge retrieval (long-context reading comprehension), while MemoryBench is the first to systematically simulate and evaluate procedural memory built from accumulated user feedback, which is central to true continual learning.

The taxonomy of memory (declarative/procedural, semantic/episodic) and feedback (explicit/implicit, verbose/action) is clearly motivated by neuroscience and IR literature and is used consistently to organize both dataset construction and analysis (Table 1, Table 3).

Very comprehensive benchmark construction: 11 public datasets spanning 3 domains, 2 languages, and 4 task formats (LiSo/SiLo/LiLo/SiSo) with ~20k cases, substantially broader than prior LLM memory benchmarks that are mostly restricted to long-input-short-output reading comprehension.

Extensive and carefully designed experimental protocol: both off-policy and on-policy settings, multiple backbone LLMs (Qwen3-8B/32B, Mistral3.2-24B) for both the system-under-test and the user simulator, ablations on noisy feedback (two different noise-injection schemes), action-feedback experiments, and an SFT baseline.

Detailed efficiency analysis (Figure 4, Table 19) reveals a practically important and underexplored limitation of SOTA memory systems (e.g., MemoryOS's >17s memory construction time per case, Mem0's catastrophic slowdown on large corpora documented with concrete timing curves), which is valuable evidence for the community.

The central empirical finding — that SOTA memory-based LLM systems (A-Mem, Mem0, MemoryOS) fail to consistently outperform naive RAG baselines once evaluated beyond narrow long-context QA — is a meaningful and somewhat provocative contribution that challenges claims in prior papers, and the authors provide a thoughtful diagnosis (declarative-memory-centric design failing to handle procedural feedback logs).

Strong reproducibility commitment: open-sourced data processing scripts, user simulators, evaluation pipelines, baseline implementations, and released simulated feedback logs to support future off-policy learning research; extensive appendix documents exact prompts for feedback simulation and metric aggregation.

Human annotation study and a qualitative case study (Table 23) are included to validate feedback quality and illustrate concrete failure modes of retrieval, adding useful triangulating evidence beyond aggregate metrics.
weaknesses: The human evaluation validating feedback-simulation quality reports quite low Fleiss' Kappa (0.093 for Naturalness, 0.380 for Relevance, 0.273 for Overall Quality), which weakens the strength of the claim that simulated feedback is 'indistinguishable' from human feedback — low inter-annotator agreement could reflect genuine ambiguity/noise in the comparison rather than true equivalence, and this caveat deserves more discussion in the main text rather than being framed positively in the abstract/intro.

The probabilistic action-feedback model (like/dislike/copy rates, sigmoid hyperparameters) is calibrated from a small number of external studies (Shuster et al. 2022; Chatterji et al. 2025) whose populations and platforms differ substantially from the tasks in MemoryBench (e.g., legal/academic writing vs. general chat), so the resulting action probabilities may not transfer well to the benchmark's specific domains.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-judge for both feedback generation/scoring and final evaluation (merging multiple metrics into a single 1-10 score) introduces circularity/self-preference risk, since the same class of models generate, judge, and are evaluated within the pipeline; the paper does not report judge-model sensitivity analysis (e.g., using different judge LLMs for final scoring) at comparable depth to the backbone-LLM ablation.

Dataset sampling for domain/task partitions is capped at 250 instances per dataset with substantial size disparities across the 11 source datasets (from 82 to 2505 instances), and this uneven contribution is not addressed via weighting, which could bias the aggregated min-max/Z-score comparisons toward better-represented datasets or tasks.

Some baselines (notably Mem0) are silently excluded from certain domain/task partitions due to runtime failures, which, while transparently disclosed, means the cross-baseline comparison is not run on a fully consistent set of test conditions for all systems, complicating direct comparison in Figure 3.

The paper's contribution is primarily an empirical benchmark and taxonomy rather than a new algorithmic advance; while this is appropriate for a benchmark paper, the taxonomy itself (declarative vs procedural, semantic vs episodic) is a fairly direct adaptation from existing psychology/IR literature rather than a novel conceptual framework.

The main results in Figure 3 lack error bars/statistical significance testing despite per-dataset standard deviations being available in the appendix tables, making it harder to assess whether the reported differences between memory-based systems and RAG baselines are statistically robust rather than noise.
